articles.headline: NFL breaks its silence on Troy Aikman and Joe Buck
keyFacts: NFL chief media officer Hans Schroeder stated on Wednesday that the league has no concern regarding reported tension between broadcasters Joe Buck and Troy Aikman.
Reports indicated that Buck and Aikman argued prior to an October broadcast regarding Aikman's expiring contract and a lack of formal renewal offers from ESPN.
Schroeder stated that the NFL is not involved in Aikman's contract situation and praised the broadcast duo's coverage of Monday night's game.
body: ESPN/ABC Monday Night Football commentators Joe Buck, left, and Troy Aikman before the Detroit Lions vs. Las Vegas Raiders game at Ford Field, Monday, Oct. 30, 2023. Joe Buck and Troy Aikman have been one of the most stable broadcast booths in sports for more than two decades, but things have gotten a little awkward between the ESPN duo lately. Aikman’s contract situation has hung over the Monday Night Football booth all season, and the two reportedly argued about it before a recent broadcast.

While it might be a massive storyline in the NFL media sphere, the NFL doesn’t seem to be worried about it. On Wednesday, league chief media officer Hans Schroeder said that the NFL has “no concern” about the relationship, pointing to the pair’s call of Monday night’s 49ers-Commanders game as proof.
Contract Tension
Last week, Ryan Glasspiegel of Front Office Sports reported that Buck and Aikman argued ahead of ESPN’s Oct. 12 Rams-Bills broadcast , after Buck raised the subject of his new contract with Aikman.
ESPN signed Buck to a significant contract extension back in September, but Aikman is in the final year of his deal, and he has not received a formal offer from the network.
Aikman didn’t deny the argument, and he has made it clear that he believes ESPN is preparing to move on without him.

“It just seems to be where they’re going — that they’re gonna go in a different direction because there’s been no talks, no contract negotiations,” Aikman told Jimmy Traina, via Awful Announcing . “We’re in a Super Bowl year. The Super Bowl is Feb. 14. My contract ends in March. It just doesn’t seem logical that if they were gonna keep me, something wouldn’t be in place before that.”

And according to a report from In Touch Weekly, the argument may have been more heated than it first seemed. An anonymous source told the outlet that it “nearly got physical off air,” and that the two were “very close from coming to blows.”
The source also claimed that Buck “never said a word to Troy” about his new deal, calling it “the biggest betrayal anyone in the industry can remember.”
If ESPN does move on, Puck’s John Ourand has reported that his sources expect Greg Olsen to replace Aikman .
‘No Concern’

As the story has grown, the NFL has now officially addressed the incident. When asked about the tension on Wednesday, Schroeder pointed to Monday night’s game, in which the 49ers held on for a 23-17 win over the Commanders.

“No concern. I don’t know if you watched the game on Monday night. It was an incredible game, right? It was an incredible game and incredible coverage by Joe and Troy, just like they always do,” Schroeder said, via Mark Maske of Front Office Sports .
Schroeder also made it clear that the league isn’t going to get involved in Aikman’s contract situation.

“So, look, that’s something… that we’re really not involved with,” Schroeder said. “I think the fans are deserving of first-class game production, which Joe and Troy have, I think, going back to ’02 or something was their first year, a history of doing that as well as anyone.”

“And I think you’ll continue to see them do that as well as anyone. I thought it was awesome Monday night. And so we’re incredibly excited about the year… and the Super Bowl and their coverage,” Schroeder added. “They’re going to do an unbelievable job.”
Buck and Aikman are set to call Super Bowl LXI for ESPN and ABC in February. It’s certainly an awkward situation, but it sounds like the NFL is content with things moving forward as planned.

articles.headline: Goal, assist... goal-kick - Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials
keyFacts: Harry Kane delivered a strong performance during Bayern Munich's 2-2 draw with Arsenal in the Champions League.
Kane scored a penalty and contributed an assist, bringing his career tally of goals against Arsenal to 16.
The winner of the Ballon d'Or, for which Kane is considered a frontrunner, will be announced on Monday.
body: - Published
Even by Harry Kane's remarkable standards, this was mightily impressive.

There were fewer than 25 minutes on the clock during Bayern Munich's thrilling 2-2 draw with Arsenal in the Champions League when the forward took matters into his own hands in a bid to break the deadlock.
As the Premier League champions prepared to defend a Bayern goal-kick, Kane seized the initiative by launching his side up the pitch with a raking 80-yard pass.
It was a moment of remarkable ingenuity from the England international, one that almost ended with Bayern taking the lead.
"Under Vincent Kompany, he has been given a level of trust that he has probably never had before under any other manager," former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport.
"For all the things we've seen him do and the positions we've seen him roam into, nobody has seen him take a goal-kick before.

"But even someone like Manuel Neuer, who is his senior and has been at Bayern for a large part of his career, sees Harry Kane put the ball down and thinks, 'OK, sure'. He lets Harry go for it because he thinks whatever he sees is going to be correct.
"At the same time, there were Bayern players running forward because they knew that the ball could come.

"For him to be taking a goal-kick is not something you may want to see very often. You don't necessarily want your number nine to be THAT deep, but the nature of his game when he is playing for Bayern is to roam, and today it was a huge benefit to the team."
Although Kane was denied the opportunity to add another outstanding assist to his already impressive catalogue, he did not have to wait long to make another decisive contribution.
After Eberechi Eze had put Arsenal ahead, Kane helped Bayern restore parity, bending a sumptuous pass around Jurrien Timber for Alphonso Davies to finish.
The England captain then fired the hosts in front from the penalty spot midway through the second half, taking his career tally of goals against Arsenal to 16.
But Declan Rice struck late on to earn Arsenal a share of the spoils.
'When you play against him, you see how much of a pain it is'
For Kane, it was another mesmerising performance that underlined his credentials as the frontrunner for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

The former Tottenham Hotspur captain, 33, could become the first Englishman since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the prestigious individual award, with Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Paris St-Germain forward and current holder Ousmane Dembele among the favourites.
Kane was named on the 30-man shortlist in September, with the winner due to be announced on Monday following a vote by an international jury of 100 journalists.
"He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves. The year he has had has been remarkable," Arsenal and England midfielder Declan Rice told TNT Sports.
"When you play with him, you realise how good he is, and when you play against him, you see how much of a pain it is.
"He is ridiculous, such a good player, and I am lucky I can play with him, not so lucky I have to play against him."
By scoring against Arsenal on Wednesday night, Kane became only the second player in Champions League history to find the net in 10 consecutive matches.
The only other player to achieve the feat was five-time Ballon d'Or winner Cristiano Ronaldo, who scored in 11 successive matches for Real Madrid between June 2017 and April 2018.

"Kane certainly looks at home at Bayern. He understands the team and its system, and they all understand him. They know that when he gets the ball at his feet, wherever that may be, something good can happen," Onuoha added.
"I think all the Bayern players are really playing into that, but then Harry steps up and scores a penalty as well.

"Having freedom is probably the best way to describe what he has got playing for Bayern, because he will work hard defensively, which allows him the freedom to be creative when he is in attack. For now, he certainly is thriving."
Kane's goal against Arsenal took his tally to 156 in 158 appearances since joining Bayern Munich from Tottenham in 2023.
It was another night to remember for the England captain, but the best could yet be to come, with the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London looming.
"It would be amazing to win," said Kane afterwards. "The voting closed a long time ago so there's nothing I can do, just wait and see what happens."

articles.headline: German youth plan France-style mass protests
keyFacts: German youth initiative "Gen Z regelt" has called for mass protests across 21 German cities on Saturday, October 31.
Thousands of demonstrators are expected to protest issues including broken schools, austerity, the cost of living, and climate change.
Organizers stated they oppose all violence, while police union official Andreas Roßkopf warned officers will firmly confront any riots.
body: "Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.

French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.

Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.

Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "state, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."

articles.headline: AOC launching search for as many as 80K ‘inactive’ NYC voters to cast ballots ahead of midterm elections
keyFacts: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez launched an effort to find over 80,000 inactive New York City voters for upcoming elections.
Her campaign said mobilizing these voters helps Democrats win the House, but an expert said many moved or died.
Campaign staff will hold a training session on Monday to teach supporters how to mobilize inactive voters.
body: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is urging her activist followers to help her find as many as 80,000 “inactive” city voters so they can cast ballots in the upcoming elections to support Democrats.

A voter’s registration status automatically changes to inactive if the voter either does not vote in two successive federal elections or fails to respond to a notice from the Board of Elections about an address change.

“These voters are at risk of being purged from the voter file. In New York City alone, there are over 80,000 inactive voters,” Team AOC said in a note to supporters about the “New York City edition” of her “Project Reactivation” program.
“This does not prevent you from voting. Your name will still appear in the poll pads and you could still vote on the machines,” said BOE spokesman Vincent Ignizio.
“But, if you are in inactive status and you miss two successive federal elections, the law says that you are then removed from the rolls and you would have to re-register to vote.”
AOC’s campaign staff is holding a training session on Monday on how to mobilize “the most unlikely voters.”

“The stakes are too damn high,” said the AOC email blast, which was obtained by the Post. “Every Democrat’s vote must be counted so we are calling on you to join us for a training in New York City on how YOU can help inactive voters protect their right to vote and update their registration status from inactive to active.
“The pathway to win back the House is increasingly proving to be through New York State.”
The move comes as AOC is feeling out a 2028 run for president or US Senate, recently embarking on an upstate tour to Buffalo, Syracuse, Binghamton and Ithaca.
Her upstate trip included launching the “inactive voter training” program.
Ocasio-Cortez, who represents parts of Queens and The Bronx, is now focusing on finding inactive voters on her her home turf with Project Reactivation NYC.
Voting experts said it will be tough sledding because many or even a majority of the people on the inactive voting list are no longer local — or no longer with us.
“In most cases they moved or they died,” said Jerry Skirnik, senior consultant with Engage Voters US, which maintains voter databases and sells them to clients.

Skurnik said many candidates don’t buy inactive voting lists because they aren’t are reliable, easily reachable and it’s not worth the expense.

The BOE’s Ignizio said the number of inactive voters remains about the same each year, with some voters being taken off the list with evidence that they moved or died, while others are added to the inactive list.

articles.headline: Lenovo's MacBook Neo rival has landed a month early — but is it worth your money?
keyFacts: Lenovo's Snapdragon-powered IdeaPad Vibe 14Q8X12 is now on sale globally a month ahead of its previously announced schedule.
US pricing for the base model starts at $799.99, which is $100 higher than Lenovo's initial promise and the base MacBook Neo.
The Vibe outperforms Apple's MacBook Neo in ports, keyboard backlighting, and RAM options, but features soldered memory and a lower-quality screen.
body: - Lenovo's Snapdragon-based IdeaPad Vibe 14Q8X12 is on sale a month before its promised date
- US pricing starts at $799.99 for 8GB and 256GB, $100 above both Lenovo's IFA promise and the base MacBook Neo
- It beats the Neo on ports, keyboard backlighting, colors, and RAM ceiling, but its memory is soldered, and its 400-nit, 45% NTSC screen trails Apple's device

Lenovo's IdeaPad Vibe 14Q8X12, the Snapdragon-powered version of the colorful laptop it pitched at IFA 2026 as an answer to Apple's MacBook Neo, is now on sale through Lenovo's own web stores in the US, UK, Canada, the Eurozone, Malaysia and Singapore.
That puts it just barely a month ahead of the November 2026 window Lenovo gave in Berlin in September, as Notebookcheck reports, with pre-orders due to start shipping on October 28.

The early arrival is the good news, but its price tag is the catch. Lenovo announced the Vibe range at $699.99, matching the MacBook Neo to the dollar. In the US, the Snapdragon model actually starts at $799.99 on Lenovo's product page, with 8GB of RAM and a 256GB SSD.
A month early, a hundred dollars late?

The timing of Lenovo's original price matters. Apple launched the MacBook Neo at $599 in March, then raised it to $699 on June 25 as the AI-driven memory shortage pushed up component costs. Apple said it had "never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly." Lenovo's $699.99 arrived in September as a deliberate match for the post-hike Neo.

At $799.99, the Vibe now costs about $100 more than the base Neo, and the same as Apple's 512GB model with Touch ID, which doubles the storage Lenovo gives US buyers. Lenovo has not directly addressed the increase. TechRadar saw this coming when the Vibe leaked in August, betting that even after Apple's price rise, "the Lenovo machine's going to be a fair bit more expensive." In the US, at least, our assessment has come full circle.

The math is kinder elsewhere, often helped along by Apple's pricing: Lenovo sells the laptop for £780 in the UK, and outside North America it ships with 512GB of storage by default. That is £81 more than the base Neo's post-hike £699, but with twice the storage. Canadian buyers pay CAD 1,099, Eurozone pricing runs from €849 to €999 depending on the country, and Malaysia and Singapore are priced at MYR 4,939 and SGD 1,379, respectively. Some Eurozone markets are limited to 8GB of RAM, and a few UK configurations currently quote four to five weeks for delivery.

For perspective, the AMD-powered 14-inch Vibe, which arrived on schedule this month, starts at $899 in the US with a Ryzen AI 7 445, the same 8GB of RAM, and 256 GB of storage. The Snapdragon model is the cheapest route into a 14-inch Vibe in the US; it's just not as cheap as was originally promised.

Upgradeability was a big part of Lenovo's pitch, and the AMD Vibe models deliver it with two SO-DIMM slots, while the Snapdragon model does not. This makes it a no-upgrades-possible offering right now, so the base 8GB is more of a commitment than it looks.
Stacking against the incumbent: Apple's MacBook Neo
The Vibe ekes out some impressive wins; it beats the Neo in connectivity: the Vibe has two USB-C ports, two USB-A ports, HDMI, a microSD reader, and a headphone jack.

The Neo makes do with two USB-C ports, one of them running at USB 2 speeds, plus a headphone jack, an allocation we have previously criticized as the bare minimum. Lenovo also offers an optional backlit keyboard, something the Neo lacks entirely, and a memory ceiling of 24GB against the Neo's fixed 8GB.
The Vibe comes in seven Pantone-developed shades, from Spicy Gold to Zen Green, with color-matched keycap sets sold separately.

"Color is the most personal design decision people make when choosing a device," Lenovo's Brian Leonard said at launch, that "versatility is certainly the big advantage of the IdeaPad Vibe" over Apple's machine.

Build quality is less clear-cut, however: metal configurations use aluminum for the lid and base, but the palm rest, keyboard deck and trackpad are plastic, and cheaper builds swap in a plastic bottom cover. HotHardware, which handled it at IFA, judged that the Vibe out-specs the Neo but added, "I don't think it feels as premium, and that's unfortunate." The Vibe also uses a fan, whereas the Neo is silent, opting for a fanless design.

The Neo set a high bar; we previously called it "the best budget laptop you can buy right now" at launch, though the $100 increase has since made it harder to recommend to everyone, with a potential argument that can be made that multiple budget Windows 11 laptops are now often the better buy.

At $799.99 in the US, it is a tough sell as a MacBook Neo alternative. For the same money, you get a Neo with 512GB of storage and Touch ID, a sharper, brighter screen, and Apple's arguably more mature software running on its own silicon. The Vibe's case rests on ports, a backlit keyboard, a slightly larger screen, and the option of 16GB or 24GB of RAM, which the Neo cannot offer at any price. If those matter to you, it is a reasonable Windows laptop with a lot of personality. It is just not the $699 Neo-matcher Lenovo announced earlier.

articles.headline: U.S. ordering some staff to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
keyFacts: The U.S. State Department ordered non-emergency government personnel and family members to depart Saudi Arabia following attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants.
Houthi strikes on Saudi civilian and oil infrastructure threaten regional stability and global oil flows through the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
President Trump stated that the U.S. may conduct strikes on the Houthis, while a Yemeni official warned attacks will continue unless confronted.
body: The U.S. State Department has ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia, following an by Iran-backed Houthi militants.

The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran, a U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday.

The State Department "issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote in a Wednesday X post, pushing back on a report that orders could apply to other Gulf states.

CBS News has learned several other embassies adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, but have not gone on ordered departure, which involves the mandatory evacuation of designated diplomatic staff and accompanying family due to security risks.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.

The decision to draw down personnel in Saudi Arabia comes after U.S. embassies in the kingdom, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries , urging Americans in the region to exercise caution and prepare for travel disruptions due to Houthi attacks.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott said Wednesday.

The Houthis have launched drones and missiles at airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including a earlier this month that killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. One American was among those killed.
The attacks have continued, with a Saudi-led military coalition reporting that it intercepted multiple Houthi drones on Monday and Tuesday.

Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said Tuesday that air defenses blocked a drone attack on the country's Shaybah oil field. Two people were killed and two were injured by falling debris, according to the agency, which did not specify who launched the drone.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have sought to expand their territorial control in Yemen. The group has controlled a large swath of the country for more than a decade, including the capital of Sanaa.
Some Saudi officials have blamed Iran for the conduct of the Houthis, which are aligned with the Islamic Republic. Iran has denied any role in the escalation.

The conflict could cause problems beyond Saudi Arabia due to the Houthis' proximity to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key maritime chokepoint that a large share of the world's oil flows through. The strait has become more important in recent months due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz wrought by the U.S.-Iran war.
Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to the Foreign Minister of Yemen, warned in an interview with CBS News on Tuesday that the Houthis could continue their attacks unless confronted.
"We are fighting on behalf of everyone, because the threat and risk of the Houthis will expand," Noman said, adding that the Yemeni government is seeking international assistance.
The United Kingdom has offered support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive air operations.

It's not clear whether the Trump administration is also planning to assist Saudi Arabia. President Trump did not rule out strikes on the Houthis after the group's deadly Oct. 10 attack on the Riyadh airport, telling reporters: "We may."
Mr. Trump said earlier this month: "We have communication with the Houthis, and we'll see what happens. But what they did was very bad."

articles.headline: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
keyFacts: The US announced the suspension of eight technology firms, including Microsoft and Infosys, from hiring skilled international workers through the PERM visa pathway.
Industry associations and firms stated that the business impact will be minimal because many companies have reduced their dependence on H-1B visas and hire locally.
Experts and affected workers noted that the restriction creates human-level uncertainty and anxiety for Indian professionals seeking permanent US residency.
body: - Published

For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.
But that may end soon.

Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.

New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.
Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (Â£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.
"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.

Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.

A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.
BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.
Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.
But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.

A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.

"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.
Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.
While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".

While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.

Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.
Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.
While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".
Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.
The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.

But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.
Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.
Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."
While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.

Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.

Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.

Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.

"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.

Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

body: Dominique “SonicFox” McLean has backed out of Nexcon 2026 after seeing promotional material for the event that used AI to generate the fighting game pro’s likeness. The flyer seemed entirely AI-generated, including slopified renderings of other creators who would be in attendance. articles.headline: ESPN insider blasts Lakers' Luka Doncic over one major flaw he must fix this season in LA

body: The Los Angeles Lakers are officially entering the post-LeBron James era, as he made his debut with the Philadelphia 76ers on Tuesday night. Now, all eyes are on Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves as they look to take the reins of the franchise.

Doncic saw some action during the preseason, but LA was primarily focused on keeping him rested for the regular season. It is also worth noting that Doncic received a technical foul during the preseason.
“Annnnnnnnd we have a preseason technical foul on Luka Doncic. You may recall Luka getting suspended for techs last spring,” The Athletic’s Law Murray wrote.

Doncic has enjoyed his first two seasons with the Lakers, and this one doesn't seem like it will be any different. The guard has been vocal this offseason about his feelings toward LA. Just hours before the team's season opener against the Golden State Warriors, Doncic sent a message to the fans.
“Dear LA, Tonight we start our run for a championship. Every player dreams of holding that trophy. To do it for all of you amazing fans would mean everything to us," Doncic said.

The superstar wants to give his all for the Lakers this season and prove he has what it takes to lead the team. Doncic is also aiming to play in every game this season. However, after he publicly made that goal clear, ESPN’s Brian Windhorst criticized him for how often he argues with officials.
“When you say 'I'm not gonna take a night off’, are you going to take possessions off because you're complaining to the officials,” Windhorst said.

Last season, Doncic was suspended for a game after exceeding the NBA's technical foul limit during the regular season. With the veteran already picking up a technical for arguing with a referee during the preseason, it highlights one of the biggest areas of his game that needs improvement.

Playing every night could increase the risk of accumulating more technical fouls, especially given his tendency to argue with officials. Doncic needs to show real growth in this area, particularly if he wants the Lakers to succeed this season.

articles.headline: The 10 best alchemy cards in Magic: The Gathering, ranked
keyFacts: Wizards of the Coast announced that the Magic: The Gathering digital format Alchemy is officially scheduled for retirement in early 2027.
Launched in 2021, Alchemy expanded mechanical design by allowing digital-native mechanics and overnight card rebalancing on MTG Arena.
Cards like Forsaken Crossroads, Town-Razer Tyrant, and Crucias, Titan of the Waves defined the format through digital-only mechanics and rebalancing adjustments.
body: The most polarizing experiment in Magic: The Gathering history is drawing to a close. When Wizards of the Coast launched Alchemy on MTG Arena in 2021, it promised a digital-native frontier, a platform where cards could be rebalanced overnight and mechanics like Conjure, Seek, and Perpetual could operate unburdened by tabletop constraints. Now, with Wizards officially setting the format's retirement for early 2027, Arena’s most ambitious design sandbox is entering its final chapter.

Love it or hate it, Alchemy fundamentally expanded Magic’s mechanical lexicon. It proved a digital platform that could just as easily test ideas physically impossible on cardboard as much as it simulated paper play. Drafting the Power Nine from thin air, altering card stats permanently across zones, and directly patching first-player win-rate disparities horrified MTG purists, yet it also gave digital players a hyper-evolving metagame that embraced software's speed.

Though the dedicated queue is sunsetting, Alchemy’s digital footprint will endure across formats like Historic, Timeless, and Brawl. To understand this chaotic era of digital card design, let’s take a peek at some of the cards that defined it. From format-warping value engines to brilliant structural fixes, here are the 10 cards that best encapsulate Magic's Alchemy experiment.
10 Forsaken Crossroads — Alchemy: Innistrad

Forsaken Crossroads may be the least exciting card on this list to look at, but it’s also one that best explains why Alchemy was willing to experiment with the fundamentals of Magic. The land enters tapped, lets you choose a color, and you scry when it enters; if you're not the starting player, you may untap it immediately. In other words, Forsaken Crossroads is a land specifically designed to address the disadvantage of going second. That's an unusual thing for a Magic card to acknowledge so directly. Instead of pretending that the play/draw imbalance doesn't exist, Alchemy designed a card around it.

Forsaken Crossroads became useful far outside Alchemy, appearing in Historic, Brawl, and other Arena environments. It isn't a card that wins games by itself, of course, but that's exactly why it’s such a good fit for this list. Alchemy wasn't only about making broken cards; sometimes its most interesting ideas were surprisingly subtle.
9 Symmetry Sage — Adventures in the Forgotten Realms

Marking the first entry on this list that isn't an Alchemy exclusive, Symmetry Sage is inseparable from the format’s approach to rebalancing. Wizards changed the digital version from a 0/2 into a 0/3 and increased the power it could grant to another creature through its Magecraft effect, which buffs a creature to base power 3 whenever you cast or copy an instant or sorcery. The change effectively turned what was already an interesting one-drop into a far more threatening piece for blue aggressive decks.

Symmetry Sage is exactly what makes Alchemy so fascinating. Wizards could effectively create a different version of a card for digital formats without changing the physical version sitting in someone's collection. The card went on to matter most in Historic, particularly alongside cheap wizard creatures that could take advantage of its power-setting ability. It therefore represents another side of Alchemy's legacy — not a card invented for the format, but a demonstration of how digital rebalancing could alter the competitive identity of an existing Magic card.
8 Fragment Reality — Alchemy: Kamigawa

What happens when you take one of Magic's most powerful effects and give it an appropriately weird Alchemy drawback? Fragment Reality. For a single white mana, the instant can exile a nontoken artifact, creature, or enchantment, but (much like Generous Gift, Path to Exile, and Chaos Warp) the opponent gets a random creature card with lower mana valye from their library. That tradeoff is the entire point. You aren't simply removing a permanent; you're gambling that whatever replaces it will be less threatening than what you just exiled.

Despite that drawback, the efficiency was so extreme that Fragment Reality became relevant well beyond Alchemy itself. Wizards eventually rebalanced the card after a particularly nasty interaction with Leyline options that created a powerful and consistent Historic and Timeless strategy, changing it so that it could only target an opponent's permanent. Few cards better demonstrate how Alchemy was balanced around interactions that could be adjusted digitally after the fact.
7 Fearsome Whelp — Alchemy: Innistrad

Fearsome Whelp doesn't look particularly terrifying until you consider what its ability does over several turns. At the beginning of your end step, the creature can permanently reduce the cost of dragon spells in your hand. It’s a tired, tried-and-true effect found on a multitude of cards, from Dragonspeaker Shaman to the Ur-Dragon. But if your opponents happen to leave the Whelp alive after several turns, suddenly those dragons you've been collecting all game become dramatically cheaper, as the effect can snowball over the course of play.

The Whelp’s effect is exactly the kind of ability Alchemy was designed to explore, taking the familiar idea of a tribal cost reducer and making its impact permanent through digital mechanics. Wizards even included Fearsome Whelp among the early cards it chose to rebalance, a good indication of how quickly the effect could become problematic. It may not be Alchemy's flashiest creature, but it captures the format's appetite for cards that become much stronger the longer they survive.
6 Inquisitor Captain — Alchemy: Innistrad

Inquisitor Captain looks harmless on paper, but the right deck can turn it into a four-mana value explosion. Its ability checks for a huge collection of cheap creatures across your graveyard, hand, and library, then uses Seek to find two qualifying creatures, putting one onto the battlefield and the other back into your library. It’s the type of card that rewards you for going all-in on cheap creatures, turning a crowded deck into an instant source of value.

The Captain became a showcase for how Alchemy's digital mechanics could produce interactions that were much harder to predict than those of ordinary Magic cards. Wizards eventually rebalanced it alongside a number of other early Alchemy cards, like Town-Razer Tyrant, Goldspan Dragon, and the aforementioned Fearsome Whelp. Even after those changes, though, the basic idea of building your deck around a density of cheap creatures, then letting a single four-mana creature turn that density into a sudden burst of board presence, is rather fascinating and not something you’ll often find in the traditional version.
5 Oracle of the Alpha — Alchemy: Dominaria

There are plenty of powerful Alchemy cards, but very few can say they put the Power Nine into your deck like Oracle of the Alpha. When this three-mana blue bird wizard enters the battlefield, it conjures Ancestral Recall, Black Lotus, the five Moxen, Timetwister, and Time Walk ans shuffles them into your library. It’s a bit ridiculous on purpose. The Power Nine are some of the most famous and inaccessible cards in Magic's history, and Alchemy simply decided that, in a digital environment, there was no reason you couldn't occasionally play with them.

Oracle isn't necessarily the most efficient creature on this list, but that's almost beside the point. Its existence captures the freedom of Arena's digital card pool better than almost anything else. It’s a card that obviously could never function normally in sanctioned tabletop Magic, which is precisely why it belongs among Alchemy's most memorable creations.
4 Key to the Archive — Alchemy: Innistrad

Key to the Archive might be the single best advertisement for Alchemy's spellbook mechanic. At four mana, the artifact is already a useful source of colored land, but its real appeal comes from the curated selection of cards it can offer upon entering the battlefield. Its spellbook includes absurdly powerful options, such as Demonic Tutor, Time Warp, Counterspell, Day of Judgment, and Lightning Bolt.

You don't know exactly what you'll get, which keeps the card from functioning like a traditional tutor, but every activation gives you access to spells that can completely change the texture of a game. Key to the Archive feels less like a traditional artifact and more like Alchemy opening a tiny portal into Magic's enormous back catalog.
3 Town-Razer Tyrant — Alchemy: Innistrad

Town-Razer Tyrant was one of the earliest Alchemy cards to demonstrate just how far the format could stretch Magic’s traditional design boundaries. The four-mana dragon targets an opponent's nonbasic land upon entering and turns it into a ticking time bomb: sacrifice the land or take damage. That's already a nasty bit of land disruption, but the card became particularly notorious because it could punish multicolor decks that relied heavily on their mana bases.

Wizards ended up rebalancing the aptly named Tyrant more than once, eventually limiting its ability to nonbasic lands and moving the damage trigger from the opponent's upkeep to the end step. Those changes are part of what makes Town-Razer such a good snapshot of early Alchemy. It was a card that demonstrated how digital rebalancing could let Wizards experiment with effects that would be much harder to change once they'd been printed on paper.
2 Rusko, Clockmaker — Alchemy: The Brothers’ War

Rusko, Clockmaker is Alchemy distilled into one strange and deeply annoying package. The four-mana 3/3 creature doesn't merely generate value when it enters the battlefield; it conjures a Midnight Clock and keeps turning noncreature spells into additional resources. Every time you cast a noncreature, Rusko's engine rewards you with another Clock trigger while draining your opponent and raising your life total. Such a brutal combination made it remarkably difficult to race or grind out.

More importantly, Rusko demonstrates why digital-only Magic can feel so different from tabletop Magic. The card is built around conjuring and repeatable digital effects that would be awkward, or simply impossible, to execute physically. The Clockmaker eventually became a particularly notorious card in Historic and Brawl, but its roots are firmly set in Alchemy, representing the format's willingness to make an entire engine fit inside one creature.
1 Crucias, Titan of the Waves — Alchemy: The Brothers’ War

Crucias is probably the easiest card on this list to point to when explaining why Alchemy could get a little out of hand. The four-mana Grixis (black-red) creature didn't need much help to take over a game, combining a solid 3/3 body with a triggered ability that could generate a Treasure while giving its controller an unusually powerful form of card selection.

The important part wasn't simply that Crucias generated value; it let you decide what kind of value you needed at the opportune moment, turning excess cards in hand into exactly the sort of resource your deck was looking for. That made it a nightmare for opponents trying to play a normal midrange game. Wizards eventually stepped in, reducing Crucias from a 3/3 to a 3/1 after black-red midrange decks made it become one of Alchemy's best-performing strategies.

articles.headline: Blackstone’s Jas Khaira says fears over AI-buildout debt are overblown
keyFacts: Private equity firm Blackstone is investing heavily in the artificial intelligence boom by offering massive loans to data centers and funding AI models.
Blackstone veteran Jas Khaira stated that market concerns regarding massive AI-buildout debt are overblown because the debt is ultimately backed by creditworthy tech giants.
Khaira noted that recent market jitters stem from factors like rising interest rates and higher credit spreads that have increased the cost of borrowing.
body: Private equity giant Blackstone is putting itself at the center of the AI boom, firm veteran Jas Khaira discussed last week on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt.
It is writing checks via various strategies, ranging from offering massive loans to data centers to investing in frontier AI models and applications.

Earlier this year, the firm launched Blackstone N1 (BXN1), a San Francisco-based central hub for its AI initiatives. The group is led by Khaira, who relocated from New York to be at the epicenter of AI.

Unlike earlier tech cycles such as mobile or SaaS, which allowed companies to reach significant scale with moderate capital, the transition to AI requires staggering amounts of investment. That need for capital is precisely why Blackstone, with its $1.3 trillion in assets under management, could play such a critical role in this tech shift.

Khaira emphasized that Blackstone sets itself apart from traditional venture capitalists through its focus on compute financing and its ability to offer flexible capital structures, ranging from debt to equity. And it has been investing aggressively.

“We’re the largest owner of compute outside of the hyperscalers today, whether it’s investments in neo clouds, investments in data centers, and being able to use that compute strategically to support companies,” Khaira said.

For instance, BXN1 played a key role in several compute-related deals, among them Crux AI, a neocloud launched in partnership with Google to commercialize its custom TPUs, to which Blackstone committed $5 billion as an investor. It also backed four-year-old Etched, a chip startup whose rapid development has caught investor attention. Neoclouds are cloud providers that rent out AI GPU infrastructure.
Blackstone pioneered a financing structure that allowed it to lend massive sums to venture-backed cloud neoclouds by analyzing both committed customer contracts and using GPUs pledged as collateral.

Blackstone’s first such deal came in 2023 with CoreWeave, shortly after that neocloud saw demand explode following the launch of ChatGPT. Despite having only “30 million of revenue and minimal profitability” at that time, according to Khaira, CoreWeave approached Blackstone for a $2.3 billion loan.

CoreWeave was borrowing against the considerable value of its large collection of Nvidia GPUs, with Nvidia also an investor. Blackstone also grew more comfortable with the loan because CoreWeave had contracts with blue-chip customers like Microsoft.
That transaction quickly became the financing model for how Blackstone and other credit institutions provided billions in follow-on debt to CoreWeave and rival neoclouds.

“One of the primary things that we’re looking to is the nature of the customer. And if the customer is an investment-grade customer — let’s say it’s Microsoft or let’s say it’s Meta — the risk gets priced relative to that customer,” Khaira said.

Building on its success with CoreWeave, Blackstone struck other neocloud financing deals, including co-leading alongside Coatue a $10 billion credit facility for Australian GPU provider Firmus earlier this year.

Khaira acknowledged that in recent weeks, the large debt burdens accumulated by these companies and other neocloud operators have begun to raise red flags. Coreweave’s debt alone has since ballooned to about $50 billion, causing Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner to note in a recent CNBC interview, “The collateral that CoreWeave is putting up which is really only GPUs is not good enough anymore. They used that in the past to get cheap debt.”

Khaira said that on the credit side, the market jitters stem from a combination of factors. Interest rates ticked up in September, and hotter-than-expected inflation signals that borrowing costs may keep climbing. The flood of AI infrastructure debt offerings isn’t helping either.

“We’re also seeing higher credit spreads,” Khaira said, explaining that lenders are charging higher premiums on top of already higher base interest rates to finance the AI buildout. “The cost of capital to price in debt for a Meta or a Microsoft has widened out,” he added, pointing out that even tech giants with massive balance sheets and solid earnings are paying more to borrow.

Concerns about the rising cost of debt have spilled into the stock market. Shares of CoreWeave dropped over 20% in recent days, while Firmus scrapped its planned IPO on the Australian Securities Exchange at a target valuation of roughly $30 billion.
“Ultimately, the market wasn’t there at that valuation, and so I think as a result, that deal didn’t get done,” Khaira said about Firmus’ cancelled listing.
“The market is thinking what is the right price for neoclouds, what is the right price for these businesses in this moment when interest rates are moving up,” he said.
Despite those pressures on some infrastructure providers, AI companies simply can’t get enough compute to power their models. Their appetite continues to drive data center buildout.

Khaira downplayed worries of doom-mongers that the massive accumulation of AI infrastructure debt could lead to a widespread credit crisis, or worse, crash the economy altogether. “This doesn’t feel like something where you’ve got 2008 banks that are shaky credits,” he said.
Instead, he pointed out that because the vast majority of data centers are built for hyperscalers, the debt financing them is ultimately backed “by the most creditworthy companies in the world.”

Beyond funding data centers, Blackstone is helping companies adopt AI through a $1.5 billion joint venture called “Ode with Anthropic,” formed alongside Anthropic and Hellman & Friedman this year. Ode supplies forward-deployed engineers to help companies adopt AI and integrate it into their operations, starting with Blackstone’s 280 portfolio companies.

When asked if Blackstone-owned companies are seeing tangible gains from AI, Khaira conceded that “there is definitely ROI, but it is uneven.” He described technology adoption as something that could move in a “sawtooth-type pattern,” which, to skeptics, can look like an oversupply of compute before adoption catches up.

articles.headline: Chris Pratt Reaffirms Star-Lord Will Return in the MCU and Plans Are Being Made Right Now

body: Chris Pratt has confirmed that Star-Lord's return to the MCU is actively being figured out.

The beloved galactic hero has been absent from the MCU since 2023, but his last appearance ended with a promise during the credits: Star-Lord will return. When speaking with The Playlist , Chris Pratt was asked about Star-Lord's future. Pratt confirmed that Marvel has been having conversations about bringing back the character, but he's remaining tight-lipped on when that will happen.

“I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise,” he explained. “So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere.”

Of course, Avengers: Doomsday is right around the corner and has a stacked cast... but Pratt is not among the list of confirmed stars. There are some actors who are heavily rumored to appear , but haven't been officially announced. However, Pratt hasn't really been part of the rumor mill. It's possible that he will be in the film's sequel, Avengers: Secret Wars , but we will likely have to wait until next year to know for sure.

Director James Gunn has been open about having no plans to do another Guardians of the Galaxy film , especially since he is now heading up DC Studios. Still, many of the characters he adapted for the big screen still live on in the MCU. Perhaps Star-Lord will get his own TV series. Maybe a solo film... or maybe he will return with a new crew in a potential Guardians of the Galaxy 4, helmed by another director. There are a ton of possibilities, but you can rest assured knowing Star-Lord is coming back.

articles.headline: Mark Zuckerberg says Meta is 'entering a new phase' with Muse
keyFacts: CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta is shifting to a scaling phase for its Muse agent after reaching over 10 million users since September.
Zuckerberg stated that Meta plans to monetize Muse through business transaction fees, commerce tools, and AI subscriptions.
Zuckerberg predicted that Muse will eventually generate higher revenue per user than Meta's existing apps like Facebook and Instagram.
body: Mark Zuckerberg says Meta is 'entering a new phase' with Muse
He expects the agent will generate more revenue per user than the company's apps.

It's only been a few weeks since Meta introduced Muse, but the company's personal agent is already becoming central to Meta's plan to start making money off its massive investment in AI. CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that the company is already working on monetizing the agent, and that he expects Muse to eventually generate more revenue per user than Facebook and Instagram.

Even though Muse is only available in the US and Canada, Meta has already seen significant adoption of the agent. Zuckerberg said that more than 10 million people have started using it since its early September rollout. "Now that Muse has clear product market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it," Zuckerberg said during the company's third-quarter earnings call Wednesday. "We expect to grow Muse to serve billions of people."

Muse is also significantly more expensive for Meta to operate compared with its other services, and Zuckerberg said the company was already working on its plans to monetize the agent. Meta plans to build "commerce tools" that will allow it to charge businesses fees for transactions facilitated by its agent, the CEO said. He noted that shopping is currently the "most common" use case for the agent, and that people are spending an average of $200 per purchase with Muse. Meta will incorporate its AI subscriptions for people and business owners who use the agent more heavily as well.

Zuckerberg predicted that revenue from Muse could eventually surpass the money it currently makes from its apps, at least by some metrics. "The average revenue per American user for our existing family of apps users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect that Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place," Zuckerberg said.

Muse is also "central" to Meta's plans to make more money from its AI glasses, according to Zuckerberg. While the company doesn't currently "make a large profit on the hardware" it sells, adding Muse to the product will help Meta sell more AI subscriptions, Zuckerberg predicted.

Meta previewed Muse on its smart glasses last month during Connect. The company said users will be able to talk to their agent in much the same way they can currently chat with Meta AI, and will be able to check in on tasks or add items to their agent's to-do list. Meta didn't specify if Muse on its glasses would require a separate subscription, but Zuckerberg's statements suggest that at least some Muse features will be paywalled on the glasses. (The company has contemplated upcharging for other glasses features, including its upcoming hearing enhancement ability.) Muse will be available on Meta's glasses "next month," Zuckerberg said.

HARC CEO John Hall said developers can limit environmental impacts by building onsite solar and wind farms instead of relying on gas turbines.
body: A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI.
Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
New research out of Texas shows how data centers are driving up pollution.

New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim.

Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality.
“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.”

In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025.

That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite.

NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible.

Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be.

“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

body: On October 20, the CEO for "AI storytelling" company Nura Studios posted a now-deleted tribute to Amanita Design's 2009 cult classic Machinarium. I saw a glimpse of the video while it was still live and it was undeniably AI generated, but that probably goes without saying given its provenance.

It wasn't good, but then: Amanita Design is one of the most visually distinctive studios in the world. The Czech-based team is also among the most assertive, if its response to Nura Studios' video is anything to go by.

"The audacity to feed Machinarium assets to AI, make AI slop animations, and call it a love letter…," the studio tweeted of the AI tribute. "Love letters are supposed to be handwritten. This looks disgusting and has nothing to do with us or our craft."

Ouch. Under these circumstances a studio would normally politely ignore the clumsy advances of a mob like Nura Studios, whose mission is "to empower creators with a human-led AI platform to bring high-quality stories to life", and whose website looks like this:
So it's gratifying to see Amanita push back.

Nura Studios CEO Sylvio Drouin did show remorse. "We are so sorry for the post we did," Drouin tweeted. "We thought it was an homage to your amazing work and I already deleted the posts, again please accept our sincere apologies."
Amanita Design has yet to publicly accept the apology. Its next game, Machinarium 2, was announced earlier this month.

articles.headline: Russia released a US prisoner. What did they get out of it?
keyFacts: Russia released 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard to the United States on Wednesday.
President Donald Trump claimed the US gave nothing in return for the release out of respect for him.
The Trump administration recently waived economic sanctions on Russia, struck a diesel deal, and interrupted US intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
body: Donald Trump speaks during an RNC fundraising event at Mar-a-Lago on October 16, 2026. | Eric Lee/Getty Images
This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is cozying up to Russia again.

What’s happening? On Wednesday, Russia released an American prisoner , 74-year-old retired teacher Stephen Hubbard, back to the US. The US, Trump said in a social media post, “out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return.”

Hubbard’s release is unquestionably good news. But Trump is wrong: In just the last month, his administration has delivered for Russia in more ways than one, often inexplicably and despite bipartisan condemnation.

What is Trump doing for Russia? Late last week, he waived upcoming economic sanctions on Russia that he had only recently signed into law after they passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support. He also:
Struck a diesel deal with Russia, temporarily lifting fuel sanctions on the country in exchange for Russia releasing a trivial amount of diesel into the global market;
Announced — seemingly without talking to either party — a Russia-Ukraine “energy ceasefire” favorable to Russia (which has since fallen apart);
Temporarily interrupted US intel sharing with Ukraine and played a role in interfering with Ukraine’s access to Starlink, which helps power the country’s drone warfare against Russia; and
Called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced .
Last month, Trump also invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the annual G20 summit later this year, which would mark Putin’s first appearance since 2019.

What does Trump get out of all of this? There’s Hubbard’s release, but taking that on Trump’s own terms ( muddled though they are), the US didn’t give anything to secure it — which means that all of those favors have amounted to not much at all, other than papering over Russia’s role as an international bad actor and breaking with US allies in Europe.

Why does this matter? Trump’s Russia embrace comes at an awful time for Ukraine, which, as the New York Times reported earlier this month, is facing a Russian campaign to “freeze Ukrainians into submission” as winter approaches. Nevertheless, on Wednesday, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian.”
And with that, it’s time to log off…

I was delighted to learn about the US’s new national park yesterday, its 64th. Chiricahua National Park — until Tuesday, only a national monument — is the first new park in six years. Located in southeastern Arizona, it’s also called the “Wonderland of Rocks,” according to the Washington Post ; you can read more about it here with a gift link.
Have a great evening, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow!

articles.headline: Ryan Bertrand leads consortium to make £87m investment in EFL club
keyFacts: Former England defender Ryan Bertrand is leading a consortium proposing an £87m minority investment in League One club AFC Wimbledon.
The proposed deal involves Sloane Street Capital paying £16m for 34 per cent of shares initially, followed by £71m over five years.
AFC Wimbledon's fan owners in the Dons Trust will vote by November 17 on whether to approve the proposal.
body: Former England defender Ryan Bertrand is leading a consortium proposing a £87m minority investment in AFC Wimbledon.
Bertrand enjoyed a 17-year career playing for the likes of Chelsea , Southampton and Aston Villa , and is now at the forefront of a group looking to acquire a stake in the League One side.
Ryan Bertrand made 262 Premier League appearances in his career Getty
The former full-back has teamed up with British technology expert Omar Mir, who is the sole funder of the proposed minority share buyout through investment vehicle Sloane Street Capital (SSC).
In a complicated deal, SSC are looking to pay £16m for approximately 34 per cent of the club’s shares this season.
They then plan to invest a further £71m over the next five years, at which point SSC would own 90 per cent of the club’s economic value.
AFC Wimbledon are owned by supporters in the form of the 6,265-strong Dons Trust, who currently own 50.01 per cent of the voting shares at the club – designed to ensure it remains fan-controlled.
After the Dons Trust board presented SSC’s proposal to its members on Wednesday night, they will now vote on whether to accept it.

For the proposal to be approved, a 75 per cent majority is needed, with at least 50 per cent of the members voting, and that majority must account for at least 40 per cent of the total membership, with voting closing on November 17.
If the deal is successful, SSC would oversee football operations, led by Bertrand as senior football advisor, but work within budgets and processes agreed by the AFCW PLC board.
The move would also see two of SSC’s minority shareholders, investment fund boss Stuart Fiertz and sports executive Oliver Ward, joining the club’s board.
Bertrand: Wimbledon role would be an ‘honour’
Bertrand, who won the Champions League , FA Cup and Europa League with Chelsea, recently discussed his hopes of being involved at Plough Lane.
He said: “AFC Wimbledon’s story is unique in English football and it was built by its supporters. We felt at home from our very first meetings.
Bertrand started in Chelsea’s 2012 Champions League final victory over Bayern Munich Getty
Plough Lane has been home to AFC Wimbledon since 2020 Getty
“We are not here to change what this club is. We are here to help it go further on and off the pitch, for the men’s team, the women’s team and the academy.
“It would be an honour to join the Wimbledon family and help write the next chapter, and we look forward to meeting members and answering their questions over the coming weeks.”
Under the terms of the proposed deal, the Dons Trust voting rights would be unaffected.
They would hold veto control of the Plough Lane – known as the Cherry Red Record Stadium sponsorship reasons – freehold.
Other ideas floated as part of the potential investment include SSC taking two of the 12 seats on the club board, as well as an observer position.
Meanwhile, the Dons Trust would retain veto over the club’s name, badge, colours, ground and constitution.
AFC Wimbledon are currently 16th in League One Getty
If SSC were to sell its stake, the Dons Trust would have first refusal and could block anyone they deem unsuitable investors.
Also included in the terms of a potential deal, SSC would see its share of AFC Wimbledon’s value would stop growing immediately in the event of the consortium missing a payment.
Control would then return to the club within three months.
Earlier this year, the Dons Trust voted in favour of external investment as long as fan ownership and control were protected.
Since then, the board has considered more than 20 potential investors, with SSC emerging as the strongest.
As for Bertrand, should a deal transpire, this would represent his first venture into club ownership after retiring from football at Leicester in 2023.
Bertrand was capped 19 times by England, and is looking to move into football at board level Getty

Angus Fox, chair of the Dons Trust board, said of SSC’s proposal: “The deal brings at least £87million into AFC Wimbledon over five years, while the Trust keeps a permanent majority of the votes, control of the Plough Lane freehold and a veto over everything that makes us who we are.
“We have set out the factors to weigh as plainly as the opportunities.
“The board recommends a yes vote, but this is our members’ club and our members’ decision.”
