articles.headline: EA cancels unannounced The Sims project, trims the Skate team and reportedly plans to lay off 400 workers: "We're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming"
keyFacts: Electronic Arts announced plans to cut 400 jobs and close BioWare while pausing development on an unannounced Sims project.
Executives David Tinson and Cam Weber stated in a staff memo that the changes are due to a rapidly changing industry.
EA will now focus on fewer large-scale projects while continuing work on franchises like Apex Legends and Battlefield.
body: Not only is EA closing down BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect - Electronic Arts has now announced a heap of drastic changes that include cutting 400 jobs across the company, pausing development on a project connected to The Sims, and bringing together Respawn and DICE.
In a memo first sent to staff and later published online, CEO David Tinson and CSO Cam Weber first took a moment to thank employees before letting them know they might lose their jobs.

"Today, we're the number one publisher in Western HD gaming," the duo wrote. "That's an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest."

The executives then laid out some changes to its portfolio of games. Top of the list is the closure of BioWare, the legendary role-playing powerhouse behind games such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Bloomberg reports around 400 jobs will be cut as part of the cost-cutting changes, including roughly 50 job cuts at BioWare.

As for The Sims, the publisher claims it's prioritising something called "Project Evergreen" and is giving "the team more time to reach the full potential and vision for the game." To do so, the execs said they're "pausing development" on another Sims-related title called "Project Lotus." The early access Skate reboot (skate.) has apparently "had a lot of success," but the publisher is still restructuring the studio into a "more focused, smaller team," regardless.

Marvel's Iron Man game (the one that leaked recently) and a third Star Wars Jedi game remain untouched, apparently, though it sounds like we'll see fewer big-budget action-adventure games come from the publisher going forward: "Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success."

EA also re-emphasised its commitment to Apex Legends and the Battlefield series after the success of Battlefield 6. But that's not all. "We'll be bringing together our Respawn and DICE studios to collaborate on a future project." There's been some rumblings about a possible Star Wars: Battlefront follow-up this week, though EA doesn't give any more concrete details about what this game could be.

Then there's the publisher's golden goose, EA Sports. The executives said they're still committed to FC and the rest of its sport simulations, alongside two new projects that'll be revealed in the next few months - the return of Fight Night and a "brand-new, social-first open-world experience for our American Football team that we call 'Project Gridiron'".

"The decisions we’re making in our priorities, how we work, and with our portfolio reflect our belief in EA’s future. Some open exciting new possibilities. Others are difficult, especially for the people and teams across the company who are directly affected. In those cases, we will support impacted employees in exploring other opportunities within EA, and we're committed to treating impacted colleagues with care and respect," the executives added.
A group of investment firms led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund took EA private earlier this summer, in a deal worth around $55 billion.

articles.headline: Hold onto your old HomePod – an upgrade is on the way
keyFacts: Apple announced the HomePod Mini 2 with new capabilities including a four-speaker home theater configuration and Mac audio output.
MacRumors reported that upcoming HomePod 27.2 software will bring select new features to older HomePod and HomePod Mini models.
Apple stated that only the new HomePod Mini 2 will receive Siri AI features due to its upgraded S10 processor.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Apple’s new HomePod Mini 2 debuted with several new features.
- Many advanced features will be available on the 2023 HomePod (2nd Gen).
- Less advanced features will be coming to the 2020 HomePod Mini (1st Gen).

Apple announced the new HomePod Mini 2 last week, with several standout capabilities: It enables a four-speaker home theater configuration when paired with the fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, allows up to two speakers to be the default audio output for compatible Macs, has a dynamic RGB light display, and can lock the speaker’s touch control panel.
Which older HomePods are getting new features?

As reported by MacRumors, HomePod 27.2 software is available to developers and public beta testers, and may launch next week. According to the same reporting, the following speakers are eligible for these features:
- HomePod (1st Gen): Lock Controls touch panel disabling.
- HomePod Mini (1st Gen): Lock Controls; Sound Glow RGB light display.
- HomePod (2nd Gen): Lock Controls; Sound Glow; Mac audio output; four-speaker array when paired with fourth-gen Apple TV 4K.

The first-gen HomePod is excluded from Sound Glow due to incompatibility with its LED light display, and excluded from advanced audio features with Mac and Apple TV 4K due to its older networking and audio processing capabilities. The first-gen HomePod Mini’s older processing capabilities also exclude it from persistent audio streams from Apple TV 4K and Mac. However, you can still stream music from your Mac to your first-gen HomePod Mini via AirPlay.
Whole-home audio is just as valuable as Siri

The new HomePod Mini 2 will be the only HomePod to receive Siri AI, thanks to its upgraded S10 processor, the same one found in the Apple Watch Series 10, 11, SE 3, and Ultra 3. However, with Siri AI likely in your Mac, MacBook, iPad, and iPhone, it may be overkill to also have it four times over in your living room via HomePod.

Instead, Apple realized it’s just as valuable, if not more so, to compete for its consumers’ loyalty in the home audio space. So it’s letting you arrange existing HomePods in a four-speaker configuration with Apple TV 4K, or in a single or dual configuration when paired with a Mac.

While some consumers may be interested in a $1,100 to $1,300 flagship soundbar, others may be better off investing in two HomePod Mini 2s to accompany their existing HomePods (2nd Gen). It’s certainly a cheaper option. Plus, if you’re already an Apple power user, two more HomePod Mini 2s will fit neatly into your Home app; there’s no need to download another app to control a third-party surround system.
According to Apple, compatible HomePods can serve as the default audio output for Macs with Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7.

Previously, users could only use their HomePod with a Mac when streaming audio from the computer to the speaker via AirPlay. When playing audio from third-party apps or media platforms, AirPlay can experience noticeable audio/video delays.

Though the older HomePod (2nd Gen) supports an older Wi-Fi protocol, its S7 processor and U1 ultra-wideband chip can handle time synchronization, bandwidth, and audio processing for persistent audio streams.
Longevity is attractive, too

Many tech companies pledge to reduce their environmental footprint, usually by using less plastic packaging and making products with recycled materials. However, the most surefire way to reduce one’s environmental burden is to keep tech products for as long as possible, which keeps defunct products and other e-waste out of landfills.

Apple’s smart speakers do a great job of promoting longevity, thanks to the company’s unified operating system, high-performing processors, and more expensive hardware. Despite these factors’ negative connotations, they makes sense in a smart home environment: A unified operating system enables longer-term software support, high-performing processors provide headroom for computing upgrades, and more expensive hardware shifts Apple’s margins toward up-front sales rather than data collection.
